name: Pass to Top Control
description: Master passing from ankle lock control to side control. Learn timing, weight transfer, and leg clearing. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
Pass to Top Control is a critical escape and advancement technique executed when defending against straight ankle lock attacks. When your opponent commits heavily to the submission attempt, they often sacrifice upper body positioning and leg control to maximize breaking pressure. This creates a window to circle around their guard and establish dominant top control, transforming a defensive situation into an offensive opportunity.

The technique capitalizes on the inherent vulnerability of the bottom leg lock attacker who has traded superior positioning for submission threat. By recognizing when the attacker over-commits to the finish, the defender can exploit the temporary sacrifice of leg control and upper body connection. The key lies in timing the pass attempt with the attacker's commitment phase rather than attempting to power through secure control.

Strategically, this transition represents the optimal outcome from the defender's perspective in straight ankle lock control. Rather than simply escaping to neutral or accepting a 50-50 scramble, successful execution lands you in side control with significant positional advantage. This makes it particularly valuable in competition contexts where points and position matter as much as submission defense.
key_principles: Recognize when attacker commits to submission attempt and sacrifices positional control
Timing is critical - pass during the window when attacker's legs are disengaged for finishing mechanics
Maintain connection with your trapped leg while circling to prevent re-establishment of control
Use frames against attacker's upper body to create distance and facilitate circular movement
Weight transfer must be decisive - half-committed passes allow attacker to recover leg control
Keep knee bent and protected throughout the pass to prevent kneebar counter-attacks
setup_requirements: Attacker has committed to straight ankle lock finish attempt with visible arch and pull
Attacker's leg control has loosened due to commitment to breaking mechanics
You have established frames against attacker's shoulders or chest
Your trapped knee remains bent with some rotational freedom in your hip
Attacker's upper body is temporarily disconnected from controlling your movement

execution_steps.description: Identify the moment when attacker arches back and pulls heel for the finish, causing their leg control to loosen as they prioritize submission pressure over position maintenance
Post both hands against attacker's shoulders or chest, creating a pushing frame that will facilitate your circular movement and prevent them from following your pass attempt
Use hip rotation combined with frame pressure to extract your knee toward your chest, clearing your foot from their grip as their focus remains on the submission attempt
Step your freed leg around attacker's body toward their head, using your frames to push off and create the momentum needed to bypass their legs entirely
Continue circular motion until both your legs have cleared attacker's guard entirely, preventing any last-second leg entanglement or guard recovery attempt
Drop your weight perpendicular to attacker's torso, establishing crossface control and hip-to-hip connection to secure the dominant side control position before they can recover

common_counters.counter: Attacker releases ankle grip and recovers leg triangle control before pass completes
common_counters.your_response: Commit fully to the pass once initiated - hesitation allows recovery. Use explosive hip movement and maintain strong frames throughout

common_counters.counter: Attacker transitions to kneebar as you extract your leg
common_counters.your_response: Keep knee bent throughout extraction. Never allow full leg extension during the pass attempt. Direct knee toward chest rather than away from body

common_counters.counter: Attacker sits up and establishes butterfly hooks during your pass attempt
common_counters.your_response: If attacker releases for butterfly, continue pressure and pass their butterfly guard rather than disengaging. Their position change actually facilitates your advancement

common_counters.counter: Attacker maintains grip on ankle and follows your circular movement
common_counters.your_response: If grip remains but leg control is gone, continue circling. The grip without leg control cannot generate submission pressure and will break as you establish top position

common_errors.error: Attempting pass while attacker still maintains secure leg triangle control
common_errors.consequence: Pass fails completely, attacker tightens control and may advance to more dominant leg entanglement like inside ashi-garami
common_errors.correction: Only attempt pass when attacker commits to finish and sacrifices leg control. If leg triangle remains secure, work defensive sequences first

common_errors.consequence: Exposes knee to kneebar counter-attack, trading ankle lock defense for potentially more dangerous submission
common_errors.correction: Keep trapped knee bent and pulled toward chest throughout the entire extraction and passing sequence

common_errors.error: Half-committing to pass and stopping mid-movement
common_errors.consequence: Creates scramble situation where attacker can recover leg control or transition to alternative attacks
common_errors.correction: Once pass is initiated, commit fully to completion. The movement must be continuous and decisive from recognition through establishment

common_errors.error: Failing to establish frames before attempting circular movement
common_errors.consequence: Attacker follows your movement and maintains control, pass fails and position may worsen
common_errors.correction: Always establish strong pushing frames against attacker's upper body before initiating any circular passing movement

common_errors.error: Stopping movement after clearing legs without immediately establishing control
common_errors.consequence: Attacker recovers guard or creates scramble, losing the positional advantage the pass should have secured
common_errors.correction: Continue through to side control establishment in one continuous sequence. The pass is not complete until crossface and hip control are secured

training_progressions.description: Practice identifying the commitment window with cooperative partner. Focus on frame establishment, leg extraction mechanics, and circular movement patterns without resistance. Build muscle memory for the complete sequence.

Partner provides realistic ankle lock attempts with varying commitment levels. Practice recognizing genuine opportunities versus feigned commitment. Add light resistance to leg extraction and passing phases.

Partner attempts common counters including kneebar transitions and leg control recovery. Practice maintaining knee protection and completing pass through counter attempts. Develop contingency responses.

Incorporate into rolling with full resistance. Start from straight ankle lock control positions and work complete defensive sequences including this pass. Track success rate and refine timing based on live feedback.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Circle toward the side of your trapped leg rather than around attacker's head. Useful when attacker's upper body positioning blocks the standard path. Requires more hip mobility but can catch attacker off-guard.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When attacker's frames block the standard head-side path or when inside angle is more accessible

variants_and_adaptations.description: Use frames to create enough distance to stand, then pass attacker's guard from standing position. Higher risk of counter-attacks during standing phase but creates significant pressure advantage.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When attacker's leg control is completely compromised and you have sufficient space to stand safely

variants_and_adaptations.description: If full pass is not available, accept half guard as intermediate position rather than remaining in ankle lock control. Allows you to work passing sequences from more stable position.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When attacker partially recovers leg control during pass attempt but cannot re-establish full ankle lock position

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Pass to Top Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to escape straight ankle lock control while simultaneously establishing a dominant top position (side control) rather than simply escaping to neutral. This transforms a defensive situation into an offensive advantage, gaining both positional points and submission opportunities.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Pass to Top Control from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Straight Ankle Lock Control where you are the defender (top position relative to the leg attack). Your opponent is attacking your ankle from bottom position with their legs wrapped around your trapped leg and hands controlling your foot.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips and frames needed for Pass to Top Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The key frames are both hands posted against the attacker's shoulders or chest, creating pushing pressure that facilitates circular movement. No specific grips are needed - the technique relies on frames rather than grips, as your hands need mobility to adjust positioning throughout the pass.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you counter Pass to Top Control when attacking the ankle lock?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary counter is recognizing the pass attempt early and recovering leg triangle control before the defender can complete the circle. This requires balancing submission commitment with positional awareness, releasing finish attempt if necessary to maintain leg control rather than losing position entirely.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Pass to Top Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when the attacker commits heavily to the finish attempt by arching their back and pulling your heel, which temporarily sacrifices their leg control and upper body positioning. This commitment window typically lasts 2-4 seconds and represents the highest-percentage opportunity for the pass.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must you keep your knee bent during the leg extraction phase?
knowledge_assessment.answer: A bent knee protects against kneebar counter-attacks that become available when the leg straightens. Full leg extension creates a direct line for the attacker to transition to kneebar, potentially trading one leg attack for another. Keeping the knee bent and directed toward your chest maintains structural protection throughout the pass.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent starts arching for the finish but keeps one leg wrapped around yours - what adjustment do you make?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If one leg remains wrapped, use your frame pressure to control their upper body while using your free leg to push down on their wrapping leg and create separation. Clear the wrapping leg before attempting the full circular pass. Attempting to circle with partial leg control remaining typically fails.

knowledge_assessment.question: What immediate actions must you take after clearing your legs past the attacker's guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately establish side control by dropping your weight perpendicular to the attacker's torso, securing crossface control with your forearm across their face, and establishing hip-to-hip connection. The pass is incomplete until these controls are established - stopping after clearing legs allows guard recovery.

safety_considerations: Pass to Top Control is a relatively low-risk technique compared to other leg lock escapes, but requires attention to knee protection throughout. Never allow your trapped leg to straighten during extraction as this exposes the knee to kneebar attacks. Train the timing recognition phase extensively before adding resistance to avoid injury from poorly-timed attempts. Communicate clearly with training partners about commitment levels during drilling. If you feel significant pressure on your ankle or knee during the pass attempt, prioritize defense over position - tap if necessary rather than forcing a pass through dangerous submission pressure.
position_integration: Pass to Top Control represents the optimal defensive outcome from straight ankle lock control, converting a defensive emergency into dominant side control position. Within the leg lock defense hierarchy, this technique sits above simple escapes to standing or guard recovery because it generates positional advantage rather than returning to neutral. The pass integrates with the broader side control attack system, providing access to kimuras, americanas, arm triangles, and mount transitions immediately after completion. It also functions as a deterrent against leg lock specialists who know that over-committing to ankle lock finishes opens this counter-attack. Purple and brown belts should develop this technique as part of comprehensive leg lock defense to maintain offensive pressure even when defending submissions.
